title: India Just Raised Gold Import Duty to 15 Per Cent. Demand Has Collapsed, Discounts Hit $106 an Ounce, and Jewellers Are Refusing to Stock Up.
excerpt: The duty hike from 6 to 15 per cent — the steepest in a decade — has frozen India's gold market. Retail footfall has cratered, dealers are quoting record discounts, and NRIs planning weddings or gifts face a significant cost increase.
body:
India's gold market has frozen. Earlier this month, the government raised import duties on gold and silver from 6 per cent to 15 per cent — the steepest single hike in a decade. The impact was immediate and severe.

Dealers across India are now quoting discounts of up to $106 an ounce over official domestic prices, up from $78 just a week earlier. In a normal market, Indian dealers charge premiums. The fact that they are offering steep discounts signals that demand has essentially collapsed.

"Jewellery stores are reporting very low footfall these days," a Chennai-based bullion dealer told Reuters this week. "Retail consumers are struggling to understand price trends and are preferring to stay on the sidelines."

## What the Duty Hike Actually Means

Gold in India now carries a combined 18 per cent in levies — 15 per cent import duty plus 3 per cent GST. For a standard 10-gram gold bar that was trading at around ₹1,53,451 per 10 grams as of this week, the tax component alone exceeds ₹27,000.

For context, when the duty was at 6 per cent (plus 3 per cent GST), the total levy was 9 per cent. The government has effectively doubled the tax burden on gold in a single move.

The timing is particularly painful. India's wedding season runs from late October through February, with a secondary peak in May and June. Families that were planning summer weddings are now confronting gold prices that are already elevated by global factors — gold has rallied 38 per cent over the past year to around $4,560 an ounce — compounded by a duty that adds roughly ₹15,000 to ₹18,000 per 10 grams on top.

## Why the Government Did It

The duty hike serves two purposes. First, India's trade deficit has widened. Gold is the country's second-largest import by value after crude oil. Higher duties reduce gold imports, which improves the current account balance and supports the rupee. With India's forex reserves already at a one-year low of $681 billion and the RBI actively defending the rupee, reducing gold-driven dollar outflows is a macroeconomic priority.

Second, the government wants to redirect household savings from gold — which generates no productive economic output — toward financial instruments like mutual funds, fixed deposits, and equity markets. India's mutual fund SIP (systematic investment plan) inflows have been hitting record highs, and policymakers want to keep that momentum going.

## The NRI Impact

For NRIs, the calculus has changed in three specific ways.

**Wedding gold is now significantly more expensive.** A typical South Indian wedding involves 40 to 100 grams of gold jewellery. At current prices with the new duty, the gold component alone costs ₹6.1 to ₹15.3 lakh ($6,400 to $16,000). That is an increase of roughly ₹2.4 to ₹6.1 lakh compared to pre-hike levels.

**Carrying gold from abroad is now more attractive — but riskier.** NRIs are allowed to bring gold into India under a duty-free allowance (currently up to 1 kg for male passengers and 1 kg for female passengers, subject to conditions and limits that vary by residency duration). The price differential created by the duty hike makes smuggling more lucrative, which means customs enforcement at Indian airports will intensify. NRIs carrying even legitimate quantities should expect closer scrutiny.

**Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs) look better by comparison.** SGBs issued by the RBI carry no import duty, offer a 2.5 per cent annual interest rate, and provide capital gains tax exemption if held to maturity. The duty hike has widened the cost advantage of SGBs over physical gold. The catch: the RBI has not issued new SGB tranches since February 2024, though the existing secondary market on NSE and BSE remains active.

## Global Context

Globally, gold has been under pressure. Spot gold fell to a two-month low of $4,365.76 on Thursday before bouncing on reports of a possible US-Iran ceasefire extension. Gold closed the month of May down 1.17 per cent — its third consecutive monthly decline and the steepest three-month percentage drop since June 2013.

The World Gold Council's India outlook notes that gold's long-term structural appeal remains intact — geopolitical uncertainty, central bank buying, and inflation hedging continue to support demand. But the Indian duty hike has created a near-term demand vacuum that could take months to fill.

In China, the world's other major gold consumer, premiums narrowed to $9–$12 from $10–$20 last week. "Not as many people want to buy at the moment as the conflict in the Middle East is still uncertain," said Peter Fung of Wing Fung Precious Metals.

## What to Watch

The RBI's rate decision on June 5 will be the next major catalyst. Bond traders are already pricing in potential rate changes, and any signal on gold policy — including possible SGB reissuance — will move the market.

For NRIs planning gold purchases for weddings or festivals later this year, the math now favours either buying in the secondary SGB market, purchasing gold abroad and carrying it within duty-free limits, or waiting for the inevitable pushback from the jewellery industry lobby, which has already begun petitioning the Finance Ministry for a rollback.

The jewellers may have a point. India's organised jewellery sector employs over 5 million people. When demand freezes, it is not just dealers who hurt — it is the entire ecosystem of craftsmen, polishers, and small retailers who depend on a functioning market.
author: Diaspora Desk
